bibl.title: Prefrontal Contributions to Metacognition in Perceptual Decision Making

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the neural basis of metacognitive awareness of one's own perceptual decisions
span.quote: In contrast, how the human brain generates metacognitive awareness of task performance remains unclear.

span.label: which brain region supports metacognitive report, as opposed to the decision itself
span.quote: Here we propose three criteria to triangulate brain region(s) functionally involved in metacognitive reports. First, activity should increase during metacognitive ratings compared to a matched control condition ( Yokoyama et al., 2010 ). Second, this activity should correlate with subjective confidence. Based on previous studies of confidence in recognition memory ( Henson et al., 2000 ; Fleck et al., 2006 ) and the link between rostrolateral PFC (rlPFC) recruitment and uncertainty of judgment in reasoning tasks ( Christoff and Gabrielli, 2000 ), we expected this correlation to be negative.

span.label: identifies right rostrolateral PFC by three pre-stated criteria, and proposes it re-represents object-level uncertainty in a form usable for report
span.quote: We show that activity in right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (rlPFC) satisfies three constraints for a role in metacognitive aspects of decision-making. Right rlPFC showed greater activity during self-report compared to a matched control condition, activity in this region correlated with reported confidence, and the strength of the relationship between activity and confidence predicted metacognitive ability across individuals.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: In summary, our results provide evidence that rlPFC plays a central role in linking decision confidence to metacognitive reports.

span.label: metacognition of perceptual decisions
span.quote: Here, we address this question by asking participants to perform perceptual decisions while providing concurrent metacognitive reports during fMRI scanning.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: We scanned 23 participants while they carried out a perceptual decision task followed by ratings of decision confidence ( Fig. 1 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: rostrolateral PFC re-represents object-level decision uncertainty at the meta level, which is what makes an explicit confidence report possible
span.quote: We discuss these findings in a theoretical framework where rlPFC re-represents object-level decision uncertainty to facilitate metacognitive report.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: object-level uncertainty signals computed within the decision circuitry are re-coded for use in report, rather than confidence being read off the decision itself
span.quote: Instead, we suggest that these studies reveal neural representations of object-level task uncertainty that may be then re-represented for use in metacognitive report.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: metacognitive accuracy arises from trial-by-trial access to internal decision uncertainty, not from monitoring one's own reaction time
span.quote: Instead, our behavioral data support an account where above-chance metacognitive ability is supported by trial-to-trial access to decision uncertainty.

span.label: a staircase equates objective performance across individuals, so metacognitive ability is not confounded by task performance
span.quote: The aim of the staircase procedure was to equate objective performance across individuals, thus rendering metacognitive accuracy unconfounded by variation in task performance.

span.label: the Follow condition is yoked to the Report condition, matching the motor act of moving the cursor without any confidence judgment
span.quote: The Follow condition was yoked to the Report condition such that half of the previous 10 Report ratings were randomly selected to specify the current block of Follow target positions.

span.label: the starting cursor position is jittered to prevent motor preparation from carrying the confidence signal
span.quote: The initial cursor position on each trial was randomly jittered around the midpoint of the scale (±12% of scale length) to discourage advance motor preparation of the confidence response.

span.label: no feedback is given, so confidence cannot be updated from knowledge of accuracy
span.quote: No feedback was given as to whether the perceptual decision was correct or incorrect.

span.label: the proposal: object-level uncertainty represented elsewhere is re-represented in rlPFC in a form suitable for explicit report
span.quote: Instead, we suggest that these studies reveal neural representations of object-level task uncertainty that may be then re-represented for use in metacognitive report. The mechanism underlying this process, particularly across different species, remains an open question.

span.label: metacognitive ability is measured as area under the type 2 ROC, distinct from type 1 sensitivity
span.quote: Metacognitive ability ( A roc ) was calculated as documented previously ( Fleming et al., 2010b ) by calculating the area under the type 2 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) using nonparametric methods

span.label: The region-wise correlations linking confidence-related activity to metacognitive accuracy were not corrected for multiple comparisons.
span.quote: We note that testing for regional correlations was carried out without correction for multiple comparisons, and thus a positive result here should be tempered by this caveat.

span.label: The study cannot separate the respective contributions of rostrolateral (BA10) and dorsolateral (BA46) prefrontal cortex to metacognitive ability.
span.quote: We note however that the respective role of rlPFC (BA10) and dlPFC (BA46) in metacognitive ability is not yet clear.

span.label: Whether the rlPFC account generalises beyond perceptual decisions to mnemonic metacognition is not settled by these data.
span.quote: Thus, further comparison of perceptual and mnemonic tasks is required to understand domain-specific and domain-general aspects of the neural substrates of metacognition.

span.label: the regional correlations were tested without correction for multiple comparisons, and the authors say the positive result should be tempered by it
span.quote: We note that testing for regional correlations was carried out without correction for multiple comparisons, and thus a positive result here should be tempered by this caveat.

span.label: some connectivity activations did not survive correction and are reported uncorrected
span.quote: Additional activations were observed in primary and extrastriate visual cortex that did not survive correction for multiple comparisons ( p < 0.001, uncorrected; see Fig. 5 ).

span.label: the respective roles of rlPFC and dlPFC in metacognitive ability are stated to be unclear
span.quote: We note however that the respective role of rlPFC (BA10) and dlPFC (BA46) in metacognitive ability is not yet clear.

span.label: whether the region serves metacognition outside perceptual decisions is an open question
span.quote: Whether rlPFC activity plays a role in metacognition in domains outside of evaluation of perceptual decision making is an open question.

span.label: a localiser scan was collected and then dropped because the main analysis found no visual cortex effects
span.quote: After the main experiment, subjects passively viewed clear images of faces and houses as a localizer for category-specific extrastriate visual regions. As our initial whole-brain analyses did not find effects in visual cortex, we do not analyze these data further here.

span.label: three subjects excluded for performance, one more from the intelligence analysis
span.quote: We excluded three subjects from further analysis due to type 1 d ′ scores >2 SDs from the group mean. Twenty-three subjects were included in the remaining analyses (10 males; age, 19–48 years; mean age, 26.5 years).

span.label: metacognitive ability did not correlate with fluid intelligence, reported as a null
span.quote: We note that in the present study, metacognitive ability did not significantly correlate with fluid intelligence ( g ).

span.label: the type 1 versus type 2 distinction, which is what makes metacognition measurable separately from performance
span.quote: Perceptual performance was assessed using type 1 signal detection theory (SDT; Green and Swets, 1966 ). We calculated sensitivity

span.label: the object-level versus meta-level model, imported as the framework for perceptual metacognition
span.quote: An influential model of metacognition postulates a dissociation between the “object” level cognition and the “meta” level, conceptualized as monitoring and controlling the object level

span.label: metacognitive ability is defined so as to be independent of task performance - measured by type 2 ROC after a staircase equates type 1 sensitivity across people
span.quote: The aim of the staircase procedure was to equate objective performance across individuals, thus rendering metacognitive accuracy unconfounded by variation in task performance.

span.label: object level and meta level are distinguished as monitoring and controlling versus being monitored, which is what makes the two separable in principle
span.quote: An influential model of metacognition postulates a dissociation between the “object” level cognition and the “meta” level, conceptualized as monitoring and controlling the object level

span.label: confidence is instructed as RELATIVE rather than absolute, because the task is too hard for certainty
span.quote: In healthy individuals, performance on a particular cognitive task and metacognition of performance are usually tightly coupled. For instance, knowing the answer to a question will tend to be accompanied by knowing that one knows the answer. Such a close relationship requires careful control over task performance to isolate a metacognitive component of behavior.

span.label: the paper distinguishes object-level uncertainty, which other studies measure, from metacognitive report, and argues the earlier work cannot separate them without concurrent reports
span.quote: However, in the absence of concurrent reports of decision confidence (e.g., post-decision wagers) it is difficult to assess the specificity with which this activity relates to confidence per se

span.label: extends → Rounis et al. (2010); Fleming et al. (2010b); Yokoyama et al. (2010)
span.quote: Our work complements and extends previous studies implicating a dependence of metacognitive ability on anterior PFC structure and function ( Rounis et al., 2010 ; Fleming et al., 2010b ; Yokoyama et al., 2010 ).

span.label: replicates → Song et al. (2011); Maniscalco and Lau (2012)
span.quote: Behaviorally, we replicate previous findings that variation in metacognitive ability can be dissociated from variation in metacognition due to task performance ( Song et al., 2011 ; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012 ).

span.label: builds-on → Fleming et al. (2010b); Kornbrot (2006)
span.quote: Metacognitive ability ( A roc ) was calculated as documented previously ( Fleming et al., 2010b ) by calculating the area under the type 2 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) using nonparametric methods ( Kornbrot, 2006 ).

span.label: extends → structural and TMS evidence that anterior PFC supports metacognitive accuracy
span.quote: We discuss these findings in a theoretical framework where rlPFC re-represents object-level decision uncertainty to facilitate metacognitive report.

span.label: qualifies → studies of decision confidence that manipulate difficulty without collecting concurrent confidence reports
span.quote: However, in the absence of concurrent reports of decision confidence (e.g., post-decision wagers) it is difficult to assess the specificity with which this activity relates to confidence per se

span.label: distinguishes-from → left rlPFC, dACC and right PPC, which track confidence but do not predict metacognitive ability
span.quote: Outside of right rlPFC, we found that left rlPFC, dACC, and right PPC correlated with confidence on metacognitive report trials. Unlike in right rlPFC, confidence-related activity in these regions did not significantly predict metacognitive ability across individuals. This difference can be explained if we assume that activity in these regions correlates with object-level task uncertainty (which on average will be related to reported confidence) but does not directly support meta-level commentaries.

span.label: contradicts → the expectation that metacognitive ability tracks fluid intelligence
span.quote: We note that in the present study, metacognitive ability did not significantly correlate with fluid intelligence ( g ).

span.label: metacognitive ability —operationalised-as→ type 2
span.quote: Metacognitive ability ( A roc ) was calculated as documented previously ( Fleming et al., 2010b ) by calculating the area under the type 2 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) using nonparametric methods

span.label: meta —distinct-from→ object
span.note: the model that licenses treating them as separable at all
span.quote: An influential model of metacognition postulates a dissociation between the “object” level cognition and the “meta” level, conceptualized as monitoring and controlling the object level

span.label: RETRACTED (A CORRELATION COEFFICIENT UNDER A CAUSAL EDGE) · rlPFC —causes→ confidence
span.note: RETRACTED: A CORRELATION COEFFICIENT UNDER A CAUSAL EDGE. The whole span: 'Indeed, in right rostrolateral PFC we found a SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE CORRELATION between the confidence beta and A roc (r = -0.47, p = 0.025), which remained after controlling for Report trial type.' A reported r and p, with a control - careful correlational reporting - recorded as `rlPFC --causes--> confidence`. Sister case to Fleming2010[4], retracted earlier tonight, where the same group wrote out the disclaimer explicitly: 'we cannot establish whether the covariation ... reflects a causal role'. — correlational; negative beta, and the strength of the relation predicts metacognitive ability across people
span.quote: Indeed, in right rostrolateral PFC we found a significant negative correlation between the confidence beta and A roc ( r = −0.47, p = 0.025; Fig. 5 ), which remained after controlling for Report trial type 1 d

span.label: metacognitive ability —distinct-from→ fluid intelligence
span.note: argued from a null, which the paper reports plainly
span.quote: We note that in the present study, metacognitive ability did not significantly correlate with fluid intelligence ( g ).

span.label: rlPFC —distinct-from→ dACC
span.note: both track confidence; only rlPFC predicts metacognitive ability, which is the paper's third criterion doing the separating
span.quote: Outside of right rlPFC, we found that left rlPFC, dACC, and right PPC correlated with confidence on metacognitive report trials. Unlike in right rlPFC, confidence-related activity in these regions did not significantly predict metacognitive ability across individuals. This difference can be explained if we assume that activity in these regions correlates with object-level task uncertainty (which on average will be related to reported confidence) but does not directly support meta-level commentaries.

span.label: signal detection theory
span.quote: Perceptual performance was assessed using type 1 signal detection theory (SDT; Green and Swets, 1966 ).

span.label: receiver operating characteristic / area under the curve
span.term: receiver operating characteristic / area under the curve
span.quote: Metacognitive ability ( A roc ) was calculated as documented previously ( Fleming et al., 2010b ) by calculating the area under the type 2 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) using nonparametric methods ( Kornbrot, 2006 ).

span.label: t-test (paired)
span.quote: Importantly, type 1 d ′ was similar for both Report (mean = 1.16 ± 0.25 SD) and Follow (mean = 1.14 ± 0.28 SD) trials (paired t test, t (22) = 0.23, p = 0.82).

span.label: t-test (one-sample)
span.quote: Decision criteria ( c ) were not significantly different from zero (mean = −0.0064; one-sample t test, t (22) = −0.27, p = 0.79), indicating that subjects gave a relatively equal proportion of face and house responses.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Between-subjects correlations between brain activity and behavior were carried out by calculating the Pearson product–moment correlation between the average confidence beta on Report trials for each PFC ROI (see below, Region of interest analysis) and each individual's A roc .

span.label: partial correlation
span.quote: which remained after controlling for Report trial type 1 d ′ (partial r = −0.46, p = 0.032)

span.label: regression
span.quote: The fit of the type 2 SDT model was assessed via the following linear regression model ( Macmillan and Creelman, 2005 ):

span.label: general linear model
span.quote: fMRI time series were regressed onto a general linear model (GLM) containing stick (delta) functions representing the onset of the stimulus and boxcar functions spanning the time of the confidence rating.

span.label: random-effects group analysis
span.quote: Single-subject contrast images were entered into a second-level random effects analysis using one-sample t tests against zero to assess group level significance.

span.label: multiple-comparison correction
span.quote: All reported activations survive p < 0.05, corrected, at the cluster level for multiple comparisons using a cluster-defining threshold of p < 0.001, uncorrected.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Analysis of perceptual performance showed that performance was well controlled by the staircase during scanning (mean percentage correct = 70.6 ± 3.2 SD).

span.label: type 1 signal detection theory
span.quote: Perceptual performance was assessed using type 1 signal detection theory (SDT; Green and Swets, 1966 ). We calculated sensitivity

span.label: area under the type 2 ROC
span.quote: Metacognitive ability ( A roc ) was calculated as documented previously ( Fleming et al., 2010b ) by calculating the area under the type 2 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) using nonparametric methods

span.label: psychophysiological interaction
span.quote: This analysis isolated brain regions that selectively increased in connectivity with right rlPFC during Report compared to Follow trials ( Fig. 5 ). We found significant increases in connectivity with contralateral PFC and occipital cortex ( p < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons; Table 3 ).

span.label: orthogonalisation against reaction time
span.quote: Model 3 orthogonalized confidence with respect to reaction time to assess whether reaction time could account for the effect we observe in rlPFC. The effect of reported confidence remained after controlling for the variance in activity accounted for by RT ( Fig. 6 ; t (22) = 2.35, p = 0.028).

span.label: Right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex met all three of the paper's criteria for a role in metacognition: greater activity during self-report, correlation with confidence, and prediction of metacognitive ability across people.
span.quote: Right rlPFC showed greater activity during self-report compared to a matched control condition, activity in rlPFC correlated with reported confidence, and the strength of the relationship between activity and confidence predicted metacognitive ability across individuals.

span.label: Confidence-related activity was exclusively negative: dACC, right posterior parietal cortex and bilateral rlPFC scaled inversely with reported confidence and no region scaled positively with it.
span.quote: Negative correlations with confidence were seen in dACC, right posterior parietal cortex (R-PPC), and bilateral rlPFC (all clusters p < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons within mask volume; Fig. 4 A and Table 2 ). No activity was found to correlate positively with reported confidence.

span.label: Metacognitive ability was statistically independent of perceptual task performance, replicating an earlier dissociation.
span.quote: A roc was independent of performance as measured by perceptual threshold ( r = −0.063; p = 0.78) and Report trial type 1 d ′ ( r = 0.19, p = 0.38), replicating previous findings of a separation between task performance and metacognitive ability

span.label: Simply moving the confidence cursor in the control (Follow) condition did not modulate activity in the confidence-sensitive regions, showing the effect is specific to genuine self-report.
span.quote: This result indicates that simply using the confidence scale (in the Follow condition) is not sufficient to modulate activity in R-PPC, dACC, and rlPFC.

span.label: Functional connectivity of right rlPFC with contralateral prefrontal cortex and occipital cortex rose during metacognitive report relative to the control condition.
span.quote: We found significant increases in connectivity with contralateral PFC and occipital cortex ( p < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons; Table 3 ).

span.label: The confidence effect in right rlPFC was not an artefact of reaction time, since it survived orthogonalizing confidence with respect to RT.
span.quote: The effect of reported confidence remained after controlling for the variance in activity accounted for by RT ( Fig. 6 ; t (22) = 2.35, p = 0.028).

span.label: The individual-differences effect was lateralized: left rlPFC showed no relationship between confidence-related activity and metacognitive ability.
span.quote: No significant correlation was found in left rlPFC ( r = 0.024, p = 0.91).

span.label: right rlPFC activity was greater during confidence report than in the yoked control
span.quote: We show that activity in right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (rlPFC) satisfies three constraints for a role in metacognitive aspects of decision-making. Right rlPFC showed greater activity during self-report compared to a matched control condition, activity in this region correlated with reported confidence, and the strength of the relationship between activity and confidence predicted metacognitive ability across individuals.

span.label: the strength of the confidence-activity relation in right rlPFC predicted metacognitive ability across people, r = -0.47
span.quote: Indeed, in right rostrolateral PFC we found a significant negative correlation between the confidence beta and A roc ( r = −0.47, p = 0.025; Fig. 5 ), which remained after controlling for Report trial type 1 d

span.label: no such correlation in left rlPFC, r = 0.024
span.quote: No significant correlation was found in left rlPFC ( r = 0.024, p = 0.91).

span.label: confidence-related activity was absent in the Follow condition, so using the scale is not sufficient to produce it
span.quote: Follow confidence betas did not significantly differ from zero in these regions (one-sampled t tests, t (22) < 1.6; p > 0.1). This result indicates that simply using the confidence scale (in the Follow condition) is not sufficient to modulate activity in R-PPC, dACC, and rlPFC. Instead, this pattern of activity is consistent with a role for these regions in representing confidence during the Report condition.

span.label: activity did not differentiate correct from incorrect trials, so it is not an error signal
span.quote: Activity did not differentiate between error and correct trials per se ( Fig. 6 ; t (22) = 1.45; p = 0.16). Furthermore, there was no significant difference between confidence betas on correct compared to incorrect trials ( t (22) = 0.18; p = 0.86) and confidence was significantly correlated with activity on both trial types (one-tailed t test against zero; both p < 0.05).

span.label: the confidence effect survived orthogonalising against reaction time
span.quote: Model 3 orthogonalized confidence with respect to reaction time to assess whether reaction time could account for the effect we observe in rlPFC. The effect of reported confidence remained after controlling for the variance in activity accounted for by RT ( Fig. 6 ; t (22) = 2.35, p = 0.028).

span.label: connectivity between right rlPFC and contralateral PFC and occipital cortex rose during report
span.quote: This analysis isolated brain regions that selectively increased in connectivity with right rlPFC during Report compared to Follow trials ( Fig. 5 ). We found significant increases in connectivity with contralateral PFC and occipital cortex ( p < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons; Table 3 ).

span.label: metacognitive ability did not correlate with fluid intelligence
span.quote: We note that in the present study, metacognitive ability did not significantly correlate with fluid intelligence ( g ).

span.label: A roc (type 2 ROC area) as a bias-free index of metacognitive ability
span.term: A roc (type 2 ROC area) as a bias-free index of metacognitive ability
span.quote: A roc is a bias-free measure of a participant's ability to link performance to confidence.

span.label: psychophysiological interaction (PPI)
span.quote: PPI is a measure of context-dependent connectivity, explaining the regional activity of other brain regions in terms of the interaction between responses in a seed region (here, right rlPFC) and a cognitive or sensory process.

span.label: three criteria for a brain region involved in metacognitive report
span.term: three criteria for a brain region involved in metacognitive report
span.quote: Here we propose three criteria to triangulate brain region(s) functionally involved in metacognitive reports.

span.label: the three criteria
span.quote: Here we propose three criteria to triangulate brain region(s) functionally involved in metacognitive reports. First, activity should increase during metacognitive ratings compared to a matched control condition ( Yokoyama et al., 2010 ). Second, this activity should correlate with subjective confidence. Based on previous studies of confidence in recognition memory ( Henson et al., 2000 ; Fleck et al., 2006 ) and the link between rostrolateral PFC (rlPFC) recruitment and uncertainty of judgment in reasoning tasks ( Christoff and Gabrielli, 2000 ), we expected this correlation to be negative.

span.term: Report versus Follow condition (metacognitive self-report vs matched motor control)
span.quote: These 75 trials were further subdivided into mini-blocks where subjects either reported their decision confidence (Report condition, 10 trials) or placed the confidence cursor in the zone indicated by the computer (Follow condition, 5 trials).

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.6489-11.2012.
